analytic.title: Mixed-Criticality Scheduling of Energy-Harvesting Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Energy harvesting is a promising approach to powering real-time embedded devices which are deployed wherever it is not possible or practical to recharge. Since the stochastic nature of harvested energy makes it challenging to simultaneously guarantee both timing and energy constraints of energy-harvesting real-time systems, the worst-case performance analysis becomes more crucial when analyzing the system schedulability. In this paper, we study the performance analysis problem of energyharvesting mixed-criticality (EHMC) systems scheduled by an energy-aware adaptation of EDF. In particular, we propose a new method that can be used to derive time demand bounds for a mixed-criticality task set, which upper-bound the total amount of time required to satisfy both the processor and energy demand of the task set in any time interval of a given size for each criticality mode. Moreover, we calculate the minimum size of the capacitor for our schedulability test to be valid. Experiment results show that our approach is significantly more powerful than previous approaches to energy harvesting mixed-criticality systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: A major trend in the design of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) is the integration of multiple functionalities with different criticalities onto a shared computing platform. Scheduling problems for such mixed-criticality systems have gained much attention in the past few years. Vestal first proposed the scheduling model for mixed-criticality workloads [1]. Based on this model, there has been much work on mixed-criticality scheduling for various platforms. These work yields interesting and challenging research problems. The major challenge is to guarantee the system schedulability at all different levels of criticality at the same time.

Unfortunately, many CPS applications suffer from the limited lifetime of batteries resulting from their finite energy availability, e.g., wireless sensor networks, industrial controllers, autonomous mobile robots. In many of such systems, it is not always practical or feasible to recharge or replace their batteries. A promising approach is to harvest energy from environmental sources, such as solar, kinetic, thermal, and radiofrequency (RF) waves, for perpetual operation. A large number of scheduling approaches have been developed to such energyharvesting setting. However, mixed-criticality scheduling of energy-harvesting real-time systems is challenging in general due to the time-varying nature of harvested energy.

Previous work has been done to address the scheduling problems of energy-harvesting real-time systems. [15] presented a lazy scheduling algorithm for such systems and determined the minimum battery capacity necessary. However, this work assumes that the energy consumption of a task is directly linked to its worst-case execution time. [9] used Real-Time Calculus (RTC) to model energy availability, but energy is the only resource constraint. [3] proposed a scheduling approach that satisfies both timing and success-ratio constraints while addressing uncertainty in Energy-Harvesting Mixed-Criticality (EHMC) systems. However, the task model where the power consumption of each task is assumed to be the same at different criticalities is unrealistic. To simplify response time analysis, [5] assumes a constant replenishment rate. Recently, [17] presented schedulability analysis algorithm to extend Adaptive Mixed Criticality (AMC) [2] to energy-harvesting systems. But its assumption that the size of the capacitor is sufficiently large is impractical. In summary, the above work only solved the scheduling problems of EHMC systems to a limited extent.

In this paper, we focus on an energy-aware adaption of EDF scheduling of EHMC systems and propose a new schedulability test for such systems. In particular, we develop a new strategy that upper-bounds the time demand for such systems, which is the minimal amount of time required to satisfy both of the total processor and energy demand of a task set in any time interval of a given size in each criticality mode. We then decide the minimum capacity requirement based on our schedulability test. Finally, low-criticality relative deadlines of high-criticality tasks are tuned using our proposed deadline tightening algorithm. Experimental results show that our method generally outperforms all the compared approaches to a considerable extent under different parameter settings. Contributions. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

• We develop a schedulability test that upper-bounds the time demand for EHMC systems (Sections III and IV), which essentially determines if the processor and energy demand of a task set in any time interval in each criticality mode can be satisfied. • To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to consider an EDF-based approach for EHMC systems under both time and energy constraints. Furthermore, an energy-aware deadline tightening approach is first proposed in Section V. • In Section IV-C, we calculate the minimal capacitor size for an EHMC system to be schedulable. • The evaluation results presented in Section VI show our approach is significantly more powerful than the state-ofthe-art under different parameter settings.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND DEFINITIONS
div.p: We begin by describing the general system model and recalling some basic definitions on which our analysis rests. The EHMC system is composed of four parts: an energy source, a harvester, a capacitor and a mixed-criticality uniprocessor system (as shown in Figure 1). The harvester draws energy from an energy source, e.g., wind, ocean waves or solar energy, and transforms the environmental energy into electrical power. The capacitor stores electrical power from the harvester. Finally, the mixed-criticality uniprocessor system receives energy from the capacitor for task execution. We assume a discrete-time model, where the smallest quantity represents an indivisible unit of time.

div.head: A. Energy source model
div.p: Let P r (t) denote the replenishment function that is actually fed into the energy storage. In our model we assume that P r (t) incorporates all energy loss at the time instant t, i.e., all harvested energy at any time instant is fed into energy storage. The total amount of replenished energy during any time interval [t 1 , t 2 ] denoted as g(t 1 , t 2 ) is given by:

For ease of computation, we can use a piecewise linear approximation of the service curve. Using this approximation, the service function can be efficiently computed, thereby avoiding the computational bottleneck involved in dealing with general curves [18]. Therefore, such curve can be approximated using a combination of several straight line segments, each of which is a lower bound on this segment of the accumulative energy trace. Then the equation of each line segment can be derived out of the accumulative energy trace. Finally the resulting form of this lower service curve is derived. In Section VI we will evaluate the lower service curve in this way.

div.head: B. Energy storage model
div.p: The EHMC system is equiped with a capacitor of capacity M that temporally stores the surplus energy. The capacitor is replenished even during task execution. We use cap(t) to denote the amount of energy stored in the capacitor at time t. We assume the initial energy level of such capacitor is cap(0) = M 0 ≤ M . We first assume that M is large enough to avoid impacting task scheduling. Since it is important in embedded applications to minimize the capacity of the capacitor, we will then discuss in Section IV-C the minimum capacity required given our analysis.

div.head: C. Task model
div.p: The analysis techniques presented in this paper may be generalized to multiple criticality levels, but we restrict the model to two levels here for the sake of brevity: HI and LO, with HI>LO. div.head: D. System behavior
div.p: Basically, the system operates in two modes: LO-and HIcriticality mode. In LO-criticality mode, we assume that no job executes for more than its LO-criticality WCET. In HIcriticality mode, we assume that no job executes for more than its HI-criticality WCET. The system model has the following execution semantics.

• The system starts in LO-criticality mode. In LO-criticality mode, jobs of all LO-and HI-criticality tasks are released. • If a job of any HI-criticality task executes for its LO-criticality WCET, the system switches to HIcriticality mode (called mode-switch). At mode-switch, LO-criticality tasks are immediately discarded. • After mode-switch, only the jobs of HI-criticality tasks are released. • If at some time instant no HI-criticality tasks are active, then the system returns to LO-criticality mode. (We will not discuss this step any further in this paper) In practice, the consequences of dropping all the jobs of LO-criticality tasks immediately after mode-switch may be harmful to the overall functionality of an application. A simple approach to tackling this is to assign all LO-criticality tasks priorities lower than all HI-criticality tasks and priorities may be assigned by EDF within each criticality, but from the modeling perspective all the jobs of LO-criticality tasks are simply dropped at mode-switch.

For such a system to be schedulable, all jobs must meet their deadlines in LO-criticality mode and only HI-criticality jobs must meet their deadlines in HI-criticality mode. For compactness of presentation we use the notation

div.head: C. Minimum capacity requirement
div.p: Our target in this subsection is to compute the minimum size of the capacitor for the schdulability test presented in Theorem 1 to be valid. To this end, such minimum size is required to guarantee that the sufficient tests based on Theorem 2 and 3 are all valid.

• We first calculate the minimum size for the sufficient test based on Theorem 2 to be valid. Since the time demand bound in Theorem 2 is calculated by using the conclusion of Lemma 7, we know the assumption of Theorem 2 that the execution units of all consuming tasks come before the execution units of all gaining tasks. The minimum size of the capacitor necessary to execute such sequence without impact on the elapsed time only suffices to execute the execution unit consuming the most energy, which equates to max τi∈τ (P i (LO))β(1). In addition, the minimum size can't be less than β(1), the amount of energy replenished during one time unit. Based on the above discussion, the minimum size in this case can be given by M LO :
div.formula: M LO = max max τi∈τ (P i (LO)) -β(1), β(1)
div.p: • Then the minimum size for the sufficient test based on Theorem 3 to be valid is given directly by M HI :

V. DEADLINE TIGHTENING ALGORITHM In this section, our target is to choose suitable values for D i (LO) for all tasks τ i ∈ HI(τ ) by using a new deadline tightening algorithm. We begin by introducing such algorithm.

Algorithm 2 presents our energy-aware deadline tightening algorithm called Energy-Aware Mixed-Criticality Scheduling (EA-MCS). The general idea is to check whether both Conditions A and B (Theorem 1) hold for all ∈ {0, 1, ... max }. If the Condition B fails for a value of , then we identify task τ i which would decrease time demand bound w HI (τ, ) the most when D i (LO) is tightened by one (Line 20-30), and tighten its LO-criticality deadline (Line 31). If Conditions A can not be met after the LO-criticality deadline of a task is tightened, then such task is removed from candidates (Line 12). If the LO-criticality deadline of some task in candidates can not be tightened any more, then it is removed from candidates (Line 32-34). If Condition A fails for a value of , then we undo the latest deadline tightening (Line 11). If there is no deadline tightening that can be undone after Condition A fails, then the algorithm terminates with FAILURE (Line 8-10). The task set is schedulable if the algorithm terminates with SUCCESS. In other words, both Conditions A and B hold for all ∈ {0, 1, ... max }. We use the hyperperiod as the bound max (Line 3). It can be easily verified that the schedulability of a task set in every hyperperiod is the same by Theorem 1, 2 and 3.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: We present an empirical investigation, examining the effectiveness of our analysis techniques. In order to compare our approach with other approaches, we let the initial energy level of the capacitor be equal to 0, i.e., M 0 = 0.

div.head: A. Obtaining a resulting form of lower service curve
div.p: We choose the solar energy as the energy harvesting source in our evaluation due to the stochastic characteristic of the solar energy source. To collect solar energy trace, we use AD7606 which is a data acquisition system with 16-bit, bipolar input, simultaneous sampling ADC to measure the voltage across the solar panel with polycrystaline solar cells which outputs at most 5V at 40mA connected to a 1KΩ load resistor, then these voltage data are sent to the STM32 launchpad by SPI. We record the input voltage from the solar panel which is placed outdoor and directly exposed to the sun during a day in June. We use the segment of 60 minutes starting from 12:00am to generate the accumulative energy input trace. On the other hand, the piecewise linear approximation of the lower service curve is implemented by a tool, called Origin [19]. Based on the accumulative energy input trace, we approximate lower service curve in Origin. Finally we derive a resulting form of lower service curve:

div.head: B. Task set generation.
div.p: Let U avg (U LO (τ )+U HI (τ ))/2 denote the average processor utilization of task set τ . Each task set is generated with a target average processor utilization U tar in mind. Then we define:
• p H : the probability of being of HI-criticality.
• r H : the maximum ratio between HI-and LO-criticality execution time. • C max : the maximum LO-criticality execution time.
• T max : the maximum period. Hence the following parameters are generated [4]:
div.formula: • L i = HI with probability p H , otherwise L i = LO. • C i (LO) is drawn from the uniform distribution over {1, 2, ..., C max }. • C i (HI) is drawn from the uniform distribution over {C i (LO), C i (LO) + 1, ..., r H • C i (LO)}. • T i is drawn from the uniform distribution over {C i (L i ), C i (L i ) + 1, ..., T max }. • Deadline is set equal to period, i.e., D i = T i .
div.p: The task set τ is initialized to be empty and repeatedly added tasks τ i , i = 1, 2, ..., with the parameters above until U tar is met.

Similar to Abdeddaïm et al. [11], UUniFast algorithm [20] is used to generate U e LO (τ i ) and U e HI (τ i ), i = 1, 2, ..., m such as U e LO (τ ) = U e tar and U e HI (τ ) = U e tar , where U e tar is the target energy utilization of task set τ in mind and m is the number of tasks which is known when U tar is met.

div.head: C. Schedulability tests investigated
div.p: We investigated the performance of the following techniques and associated schedulability tests.

(1) EA-MCS: The test in Theorem 1 using the time demand bounds calculated in Theorem 2 and 3. Low-criticality relative deadlines of HI-criticality tasks are tuned using Algorithm 2. (2) Celebi Offline EDF: The schedulability test for EDF-based scheduling of non-mixed criticality systems from [14]. This test was used to determine both (i) the schedulability of all tasks at the LO-criticality level and (ii) the schedulability of the HI-criticality tasks at the HI-criticality level. A taskset must be deemed schedulable according to both (i) and (ii). (3) EDF: The schedulability test for EDF-based scheduling of non-mixed criticality systems from [15]. Similar to case (2), this test was also used to determine both (i) and (ii). A taskset must be deemed schedulable according to both (i) and (ii).

) AMC-EWCP: Schedulability based on the response-time calculation for fixed-priority scheduling from [17], using Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA) algorithm [22] to assign priorities. We use the second response time bound calculated in [17] since it is tighter than the first response time bound.

div.head: D. Experiments
div.p: Fig. 5 shows the acceptance ratio (percentage of schedulable tasksets) as a function of target average utilization for task sets generated using parameters p H = 0.5, r H = 4, C max = 10, T max = 200, U e tar = 0.2. Each data point is based on 10,000 randomly generated task sets. From the results we can see that as target average utilization increases, the acceptance ratios of all methods decreases, but our method always outperforms the compared methods.

In the following we study the effects of varying the parameters p H , r H and U e tar . We plot the weighted acceptance ratio W y (p) [23] for each schedulability test y as a function of parameter p. For each value of p, this measure combines results for all of the task sets τ generated for all of a set of equally spaced utilization levels (0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05). Let S y (τ, p) be the binary result (1 or 0) for the schedulability test y for a taskset Γ with parameter value p:
div.formula: W y (p) ∀τ u(τ ) • S y (τ, p) ∀τ u(τ )
div.p: where u(τ ) is the utilization of task set τ . The weighted acceptance ratio reduces what would otherwise be a 3-dimensional plot to 2 dimensions [23].

We show how the results are changed by varying each of the parameters. Fig. 6(a) varies the energy utilization, Fig. 6(b) varies the maximum ratio of high-to low-criticality and Fig. 6(c) varies the probability of high-criticality. Each data point is based on 10,000 random tasksets.

The trends in Fig. 6(b) and 6(c) are relatively steady. However, weighted acceptance ratios of all approaches except Celebi-Offline-EDF go down faster in Fig. 6(a) because each task will require more energy for execution as its energy utilization increases. Among the the compared approaches, Celebi-Offline-EDF preforms very badly because it assumes that energy harvesting and task execution are mutually exclusive. An exception is U e tar = 0.05 in Fig. 6(a), with which energy consumption of each task is very low. In [15], they assume that the energy consumption and the execution time of a job behave proportional. Since the lower service curve is non-decreasing, the execution time of a job will be also lower if its energy consumption is lower. But for our method, the energy consumption of a job is independent of its execution time. Therefore, for EDF [15] using such setting, the total processor demand of a task set is lower, which increases the chance for such task set to be deemed schedulable.
In summary, our method generally outperforms all the compared approaches in all the above experiments with varying parameters in different dimensions.

div.head: VII. RELATED WORK
div.p: The first work on real-time scheduling of energy-harvesting systems is [8]. In order to characterize the availability of harvested energy, Real-Time Calculus (RTC) is used to analyze the worst-case performance of energy-harvesting real-time systems in [9,15]. The minimum size of the capacitor required for the schedulability tests to be valid is also computed by Moser et al. [15], and the modeling and analysis of energyharvesting real-time systems with limited-size capacitor are the focus of the work by Guan et al. [9].

For fixed priority scheduling of energy-harvesting systems, [11,12] present sufficient schedulability tests for different task models, respectively. An optimal algorithm for fixed priority preemptive scheduling was proposed by Abdeddaïm et al. [12]. They assume that all tasks comsumes energy faster than it is replenished. To be more general, [11] removes this assumption and present sufficient schedulability tests for such systems. Furthermore, Abdeddaïm et al. [5] present sustainability analysis for these tests and the priority assignment is also discussed. However, these works simply assume that the energy replenishment rate is constant. To address this limitation, probabilistic technique is used to characterize the availability of energy and proposed scheduling algorithms for energy-harvesting mixed-criticality systems [3].

On the other hand, both [13] and [14] focus on realtime task scheduling of intermittently-powered devices with deadline requirements. However, [13] implicitly assumes that the charging time and period are determined by the voltage threshold. [14] requires generating a schedule for one hyperperiod to test schedulability under its proposed approach. In addition, both of them have a limited assumption that energy harvesting and task execution are mutually exclusive. Recently, Adaptive Mixed Criticality (AMC) approach [2] was extended to energy-harvesting system by incorporating energy work-conserving policy into scheduling model [17], where two response time upper bounds are derived.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We develop the worst-case performance analysis techniques for energy-harvesting mixed-criticality systems. The main idea is to prove some key properties of execution sequence, and apply them to calculating time demand bounds in each criticality mode. We calculate the minimum size of the capacitor for our schedulability test to be valid. We also propose a new strategy to tune low-criticality relative deadlines of highcriticality tasks. Experiment results show that our approach is successful in practice. Our ultimate goal is to guarantee timing behaviour for energy-harvesting mixed-criticality systems. This work is a small step towards this goal and still subject to many limitations. Next step, we will extend our method to more general and complex systems, such as arbitrary deadline sporadic task systems and energy-harvesting systems with multiple criticality levels.
